title: Stage lifecycle quantile annotated notes
content:
Purpose:
Quick, pragmatic field notes capturing an annotated stage-by-stage quantile breakdown from a mixed workload run. Goal is to create a compact runbook for triaging long-tail (p95/p99) latency during normal traffic and when KV-cache is cold. This is intentionally informal — observations, small reproducible checks, and actionable hypotheses.

Context / test harness:
- Node type: rtx-a10x-large (16GB) emulated in staging pool A
- Runtime build: runtime@2025-10-28 (kernel selection + continuous-batching branch)
- Models: open-causal-7b (fp16), long-chat-13b-quant (q8) used for separate runs
- Workloads: 1) short-chat (prompt ~24 tokens, gen target 40, seqlen-emitted ~64) 2) long-gen (prompt ~120 tokens, gen target 400, seqlen-emitted ~520)
- Tracing: per-stage micro-timers (ingest -> deserialize -> route -> kv-lookup -> batch-queue -> kernel-exec -> emit -> network-egress), sampled at 1% for wall runs, and 100% for the debugging session below.

Summary snapshot (median / p95 / p99 in ms) — aggregated across 10k reqs, short-chat workload (warm cache):
- ingest: 0.8 / 1.6 / 2.9
- deserialize: 0.4 / 0.9 / 1.8
- routing: 0.6 / 1.4 / 3.2
- kv-lookup (cache warm): 0.9 / 2.5 / 4.6
- batch-queue (wait): 1.7 / 9.8 / 28.4
- kernel-exec (per-token average over generation): 6.2 / 12.1 / 29.0
- emit (token serialization): 0.5 / 1.1 / 2.0
- network-egress: 0.7 / 1.8 / 3.5
- total e2e: 12.8 / 33.2 / 80.4

Notes on the above:
- p50 dominated by kernel-exec and small batch waits. p95 and p99 balloon primarily because of the batch-queue tail and a small fraction of kernel-exec outliers (see hypothesis A/B).
- Kv-lookup is small when warm but a non-zero contributor at p99 due to occasional backend metadata retries (investigate KMS/metadata latency).

Long-gen workload snapshot (warm cache):
- kernel-exec dominates; per-token variance aggregates. Typical per-token kernel p95 spikes align with GPU SM contention windows we saw in perf counters. Total e2e p95 ~4200ms, p99 ~8200ms.

Annotated observations and hypotheses (numbered for followups):
1) Batch-queue tail risk: many p99s map to requests that arrived during a short period of reduced scheduling throughput and ended up waiting for 3+ batch formation cycles. We observed small bursts of 50–120ms scheduling pauses correlated with a background compaction job on the node (see linked artifact PR-compact-scheduler). Hypothesis: non-yielding background threads increase queue residence and cause cascades.
Action: instrument thread-level activity in the scheduler; add backpressure metrics for compaction jobs. Short repro: run synthetic steady 400 rps with a periodic 200ms compaction and sample traces.

2) Kernel-exec p99 spectrum: two distinct modes seen in p99 kernel durations — (a) long single-shot kernel (OOM-swap-like slowdowns) and (b) many small kernel restarts caused by occasional cross-stream synchronizations (we see an extra ~8ms hang per token). Hypothesis: rare CUDA stream stalls due to shared workspace contention when multiple models are colocated.
Action: repro by colocating a small q8 model and a large fp16 model on same card; add timeline markers around memcpy and stream-sync points. Consider enforcing per-model stream isolation on the allocator.

3) KV-cache cold vs warm: cold runs (after end-of-life cache eviction) show kv-lookup p50 ~4ms, p95 ~32ms, p99 ~220ms; majority of p99 KV times follow a pattern: an initial backend fetch + 1 retry after a 100ms metadata timeout. Root cause likely a small window when metadata service SLO dips.
Action: add local retry jitter and aggressive in-process fallback for small prefix ranges; instrument metadata client timings with sampling.

4) Routing thrash for feature flags: ~1.2% of requests had routing time > 50ms because of synchronous feature-flag resolution (legacy path). This disproportionately affected p95 and p99.
Action: async feature-flag resolution with default route fallback. Owners: Marissa.

5) Token emit stalls: p99 emits often co-occur with large JSON payload assembly when the output contains many tool-calls (~>15) leading to repeated allocations in the response serializer.
Action: introduce pooled arenas for serializer, and cap streaming-chunk sizes to avoid large contiguous allocations.

Investigations performed (quick wins and how to reproduce):
- Replay sampling: collected 1000 p99 traces from the sample window (11:17–11:21 PDT). Replayed them against a patched build that disabled compaction. Observed 65% reduction in batch-queue p99 magnitude.
- Microbenchmark: per-token kernel microbenchmark with synthetic inputs showed a 7–11ms tail reduction when kernel was pinned to a dedicated stream per-model. Patch PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/768
- KV-client test: added injected 120ms metadata delay in staging; saw cache cold p99 blow out to ~1.1s for some traces. This reproduces production-like metadata SLO violations.

Suggested next steps (prioritized):
- Short (1–2 days): add scheduler thread-level counters, add batch-queue jittering with 5ms randomized delay, and disable compaction in critical node profiles. Owner: Amit.
- Medium (1–3 weeks): per-model stream isolation runtime flag, serializer arena pool, and async feature-flag resolution. Owners: Marissa + Luis.
- Long (quarter): Rework KV-cache warmup strategy with background prefetch for hot prefixes and per-tenant rate-limited metadata backoff. Owners: eng-runtime + infra.

Quick triage checklist (for on-call):
- Check batch-queue histograms: If p99 > p95 * 2.5, suspect scheduler/compaction interference.
- Inspect kernel per-token tail: if spikes align across models, suspect card-level contention.
- KV-cache cold spike pattern: single long lookup followed by short retries -> metadata SLO likely.
- Routing > 50ms: search traces for feature-flag resolution markers.

Open questions / unknowns (we should answer in next session):
- Are the kernel-exec stalls reproducible at lower RPS if we artificially load other models on the same card, or do they require peak GPU SM utilization?
- Does the allocator behavior differ across GPU families in ways that make stream-isolation insufficient? Need cross-hardware sweep.

Appendix: sample trace excerpt (one p99 short-chat trace, times in ms):
- ingest: 1.0
- deserialize: 0.6
- routing: 2.1 (feature-flag wait marker)
- kv-lookup: 210.4 (backend fetch + retry)
- batch-queue: 185.2 (wait across 4 cycles)
- kernel-exec: 34.9 (per-token variance added)
- emit: 1.9
- network-egress: 2.1
- total: 438.2

If you want, I can extract a small reproducible script and a minimal repro harness (python + curl + environment variables) that runs the 400 rps with injected compaction and captures the 100% traces. Next steps I plan to take this week: add scheduler counters (today), run compaction-disabled replay (tomorrow), and open the per-model stream isolation RFC (this sprint).

Notes-to-self: keep this file lightweight; transfer matured items into the "serving-runtime/latency-playbooks" confluence page after we validate fixes.
